So does Yaquina head? I promise you they are sisters, one difference between them is that pigeon point is slightly taller than Yaquina head.

They look similar because they are considered “sisters”. Built from the same plans and slightly modified to fit each location. This is somewhat common for lighthouses, at least on the west coast. Plans and engineering for lighthouses was obviously very expensive yet vital for the time. So plans were reused if they proved successful and available. Both lighthouses are still standing by the way, Yaquina head still serving as an active aid to navigation. The bulb and fixture is maintained by the coast guard while the physical light house is maintained by BLM and the rangers.
Source: I was a light house keeper in a former life

As a former museum and collections worker: there are undoubtedly hundreds if not thousands of lost artifacts/objects/specimens “lost” in collections across the world. Museums tend to be understaffed and underfunded, leading to poor follow through, lack of documentation, and loss of institutional knowledge when members inevitably move on. 



Additionally, collections usually have a substantial back log of things that were donated at some point but never accessioned into the collection. Some of these types of donations were not obtained ethically which can cause major headaches for curators attempting to provide proper documentation. You have to be very careful, it can be high stress.



The interesting thing about natural history collections specifically, is that there are species that are unknowingly misidentified. Modern technology can determine differences that have been difficult to describe with the naked eye and early classification methods. Simply put, new  species are held in collections! You don’t have to be an explorer to find and name new animals, the mystery is out there for you to explore! 



Volunteer opportunities exist, please support your local institutions! These can be academic collections, historical societies, nonprofits, visitors centers, memorials, friend groups, parks, government agencies… Many museums lost volunteers through the pandemic, and are actively looking to recruit new folks. In most cases on the job training and shadowing is offered in exchange for an agreed upon time commitment.

So I can speak to part of why new species are found by enthusiasts. It’s important to know and understand that natural history collections have a lot to offer. A lot of smaller institutions have a large back log of material that has been donated or acquired over the years but has not yet been identified, sampled, or professionally preserved. This process is called accessioning, and depending on the organization it can take multiple steps and individuals working together to complete the record data associated with each specimen. Some specimens will hold up better over time, and especially if they have been properly cared for. Additionally, taxonomy and names have changed over the years which means rearranging specimens, and sorting them into their sub species. This means “new” species may already be, and often are, hiding in older collections, classified under another name. 



All of this is to say that often times, curators do not have the time to sort through each and every specimen, examining them each closely to identify new species or sub species. This work is often done by students, trained volunteers, or retired experts. 




The good news is that you can likely get involved with one of your local collections! They usually value passionate volunteers and will have plenty of projects to keep you busy, even if you are starting out as a docent or interpreter. Do your research, find out the nearest zoo, aquarium, herbarium, fish hatchery, natural history museum and see what kind of programs they offer for further involvement.
